summary: Registers the ENUM services email, fax, sms, ems, and mms, which use the tel: and mailto: URI schemes, following the IANA registration process from RFC 3761. This lets a telephone number in ENUM point to those ways of reaching someone. It is standards-track and was updated by RFC 6118.

plainLanguage.summary: ENUM is a phone book that turns phone numbers into internet contact details. This adds entries for email, fax, and text messages.

questions: what are enumservices email fax sms mms
what is the difference between sms ems and mms
subtitle: Registers the ENUM services email, fax, sms, ems and mms, so a phone number can point to ways of sending messages.

tldr.problem: ENUM maps telephone numbers to services through DNS records, but there were no registered names for email, fax and the text and multimedia messaging services.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the Enumservices email, fax, sms, ems and mms using the tel: and mailto: URI schemes, following the process in RFC 3761.
tldr.outcome: A number's record can now say that a destination accepts email, fax, SMS, EMS or MMS. The RFC was later updated by RFC 6118.

today: RFC 4355 is a Proposed Standard and was updated by RFC 6118. The text here does not describe the changes, so read that RFC alongside this one.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
ENUM (RFC 3761) transforms an E.164 number into a domain name and then uses DNS NAPTR records to find the services available for it. This document registers five Enumservices for the services field of a NAPTR record: email, fax, sms, ems and mms. They share one feature: the endpoints can receive discrete messages, albeit of different types.

Two URI schemes are used: tel: from RFC 3966 and mailto: from RFC 2368.
sections.plainLanguage: It adds labels to a phone book for the different ways of sending someone a message.

sections.title: Types, Subtypes and Hints
sections.content:
An Enumservice acts as a hint about the kind of service behind the URI built from the regexp field. One NAPTR record can hold several Enumservices. The registrations do not dictate the protocol or connection method. They describe what the end user will expect, and the end system decides how to do it.

The same URI scheme can serve different services, so RFC 3761 allows a type and a subtype. Here the type names the service and the subtype names the URI scheme. Even when only one scheme exists for a service today, another may be added later, which is why the subtype is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: A label says what kind of message you can send, and a second part says which kind of address to use.

sections.title: Email and Fax Services
sections.content:
The email Enumservice has subtype mailto and URI scheme mailto:. It indicates that the remote resource can be addressed by that URI in order to send an email.

The fax Enumservice has subtype tel and URI scheme tel:. It indicates that the resource can be contacted for a communication session in which facsimile documents can be sent. Clients selecting it will be able to send faxes over the PSTN using the procedures in ITU-T Recommendations T.4 and T.30. In short, they have a fax program with local or shared PSTN access.
sections.plainLanguage: 'Email' means you can send a letter to this address. 'Fax' means you can ring this number and send a paper copy through the phone line.

sections.title: SMS, EMS and MMS
sections.content:
SMS (Short Message Service), EMS (Enhanced Message Service) and MMS (Multimedia Messaging Service) are each registered twice, once with tel: and once with mailto:. Their capabilities are a nested superset. A service that supports MMS can also deliver EMS or SMS content, and one that supports EMS can also deliver SMS content.

So a client that only wants to send SMS content MAY also consider NAPTR records for EMS or MMS, since those destinations can accept SMS content. A client that can send MMS may consider EMS or SMS records too, but would have to downgrade its user interface to content that fits those services. These client behaviours are optional and are not subject to any protocol standardisation.

The MMS registration notes that MMS can stand in for SMS delivery if the SMS bearer is not supported. It adds two caveats: not every terminal that supports MMS need support SMS in the future, and there may be tariff differences.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of three boxes that fit inside each other. A place that takes the biggest kind of message can also take the smaller ones.

sections.title: Messages Sent to mailto: Addresses
sections.content:
When SMS, EMS or MMS is registered with a mailto: URI, the message travels over SMTP. The format is the one specified by 3GPP TS 23.140 Section 8.4.4 and TS 26.140 Section 4, as an MMS message. For SMS and EMS, the content is carried as either a text or application/octet-stream MIME sub-part.

Inside MMS environments, state data such as charging information is mapped to specialised headers in the SMTP exchanges. The MMS Architecture also describes an interface to legacy messaging systems that accepts standard SMTP messages. The MMS Relay Server there looks like an ordinary SMTP server to an Internet mail server but acts as a gateway and translator.
sections.plainLanguage: If the address is an email address, the text message is wrapped up like an email and sent that way.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
As with other ENUM data, DNS is a global database, so anything in a NAPTR record is visible to anyone. Harvesting can feed spam, such as junk faxes or junk SMS. A person cannot easily use a 'sacrificial' phone number the way they can with email accounts. As a principle, data subjects MUST give explicit informed consent before data is published in ENUM, and any publication may be permanent. Subscribers should think carefully before entering email addresses that reveal private data, or entering them at all, and filtering incoming messages is suggested to cut unwanted communication.

Sending can cost money. Fax calls and messages can be charged, and premium rate numbers can cost considerably more. End users SHOULD be shown the destination number so they can decide. Some value added services start charging when a short message is sent to a special number, so the terminal must show the destination for the sms:tel, ems:tel and mms:tel services. The RFC believes the mailto variants do not currently carry this risk.
sections.plainLanguage: Anything in the phone book is public. Your phone should show you which number you are about to text, because some numbers cost a lot.
